place.en: The hidden realm · Below the drop

setup.zh: 别人都往右，你往左，往下。崖底是一面光秃秃的石墙——墙后头，有风。墙脚下一汪滴水积成的浅潭，潭里趴着一只白身赤首、像龟的东西：蛫。它把那面墙护得严严实实。
setup.en: Everyone goes right; you go left, and down. At the foot of the cliff, a bare stone wall — and behind it, wind. At the wall's foot, a shallow pool of gathered drips, and in it a white-bodied, red-headed thing like a turtle: a gui. It guards the wall close.

recap.zh: 秘境里，银月领着你往左、往下；墙后头有风，墙上刻着九宫——五居中央，墙开了。
recap.en: In the hidden realm Yinyue led you left and down; there was a draught behind the wall, the nine squares carved on it — five in the middle, and the wall opened.

zh: 往左。往下。潭里，一只白身赤首的蛫。
en: Left. Down. In the pool, a white-bodied, red-headed gui.

label.en: The nine squares on the wall

text.zh: 九个格子，三三一排，边角给水泡得发白，正中那一格，比别的磨得都亮。
text.en: Nine squares, three by three, their edges bleached by water. The middle one is worn brighter than the rest.

text.zh: 石块一共九块，点子从一到九，一块不少，只是都给水泡得发黑。
text.en: Nine stones in all, dotted one to nine, not one missing — all of them blackened by the water.

text.zh: 风是暖的，带着一股土腥气，从最底下那道缝里一丝一丝透出来。
text.en: The draught is warm and smells of earth; it seeps thread by thread from the lowest crack.

story.zh:
小狰是不能带进秘境的，灵兽进了秘境，一闻见前人留下的丹药渣子便要发疯。小满只得把它寄在执事房。它死死扒着他的袖子不撒手，五条尾巴一齐竖着；周衡从抽屉里摸出一根萝卜，放在桌角上，道：「它吃一根，我记一根。」小狰盯着萝卜，那眼神分明是说「你拿一根萝卜就把我卖了」，然后松开袖子，跳上桌角，把萝卜吃了。

山门前那三百级石阶上，瞿老照旧在扫第三百级。三百多人从他身边涌下去，他头也不抬，只把扫帚往旁边让一让。小满走到那一级，放慢了脚。瞿老忽然开口了，声音不高，像是对着台阶说的：「水，退得比上回低。」小满一怔。瞿老还在扫，又道：「上回比上上回低。」小满道：「……那是好，还是不好？」瞿老没有答，把扫帚一让，让出一条路来：「腿稳。」小满走出十几级，回头望了一眼，那个扫地的老头拄着扫帚，望的却不是他，是山脚下那条缩成一线的泗水。

辰时，外门三百多个弟子挤在河滩上。泥是黑的，泥上结着一层白霜，霜上歪歪扭扭躺着几条来不及跟着水走的鱼，嘴一张一合，像是在问这是怎么回事。那道石门露在泥滩上，门缝里往外冒着一丝一丝的白气，冬天的早晨，那白气是暖的。小满隔着老远闻见了，说不上是什么味儿，只觉一闻，心里便静了一静。

石门前头站着一个人，一身灰袍，面目温和，两只手拢在袖子里，正是观主玄沉子。老弟子们说，每回秘境开门，观主都要这般站着，从开门站到进人；关门那天，又从头一个人出来，站到最后一个人出来。问他站着做什么，他说数人。可他从来不拿本子，也从来不开口数。

孙二狗挤到小满身边，两只手揣在袖子里，鼻涕冻成了两道冰溜子，小声道：「沈师兄，我跟着你，行么？我灵根差，一个人进去，怕……」他自己先红了脸，「……怕给人粘在墙上。」小满看了他一眼。孙二狗腰上系着一个蓝布包，露出一截红绳——他娘缝的护身符，小满在牛棚里见过。小满心想：跟着我，便要往哪里走，我自己都还不知道。他从包袱里摸出一根萝卜，塞进孙二狗手里：「右边人多。人多，死不了。」孙二狗捧着萝卜，道：「……那师兄你呢？」小满道：「我人少。人少，也死不了。」孙二狗没听懂，可他很郑重地点了点头，把萝卜揣进怀里，跟那个护身符揣在一处。

执事敲了三下锣。石门「嘎嘎」地响着，开了一道缝，三百多人一窝蜂地往里挤，泥点子飞了半天高。小满没有挤。人群里却也有一个人没挤——卖地图的那两个里头，踹他左边肋骨的那一个，抄着手站在人堆边上，眼睛不看石门，看他。他站在一块石头上等着——他爹教过他：一群鹿惊起来的时候，千万别往群里钻；你站着，等它们跑过去，路就空了。等最后一个人挤进了门，他才从石头上跳下来，慢吞吞地走了进去。走到门里，他回头望了一眼：那个抄着手的人，也不紧不慢地跟了进来。

走进石门的那一刻，他胸口的木牌「腾」地一烫。那一烫跟往常不同：往常烫一下，是它醒了，有话要说；这一回烫了一下，没有停，第二下，第三下，一下紧似一下，倒像是一颗心在他胸口底下跳。他把木牌掏出来，那条银色的尾巴亮得刺眼。一只半透明的小银狐钻了出来，蹲在他肩膀上，身子比从前实了些。它没有打哈欠，一双金色的眼睛睁得大大的，看石壁，看石壁上的花纹，看脚底下的石板，鼻子一抽一抽的，像在闻着什么很远、很远的东西。

它开口了，声音却变了，倒像一个人站在自己小时候住过的院子里：「……这地方。本王来过。」小满问：「什么时候？」银月道：「不知道。」小满问：「来做什么？」银月道：「不知道。」小满道：「那你知道什么？」银月的鼻子又抽了两抽，才道：「……往左。」

地图上画的路，是往右的。三百多人顺着长廊往右走，叮叮当当，声音在石壁上撞成一片。往左，是一道窄窄的石缝，缝口给一块塌下来的大石头堵了一半，石头上刻着一个歪歪扭扭的「凶」字，字底下画了个骷髅头，骷髅头的眼眶里，还有人拿炭添了两道眼泪。地图上，石缝旁边也有一行小字：「左崖，粘人。十年前粘住三个，粘了三天，出来疯了一个。」小满把地图折好，揣进怀里，侧着身子挤了进去。

石缝后头是一段往下走的石阶，窄，陡，湿，长满了青苔。走了约莫一顿饭的工夫，前面是一道断崖，崖下黑洞洞的，只听得见底下有水滴的声音，一滴，隔很久，又一滴。银月道：「往下。」小满道：「下面什么都没有。」银月道：「本王不知道下面有什么。本王知道，这里的灵气是从下面上来的。」它顿了一顿，声音低了下去，「……很厚的灵气。外头那条河、那座山、那间讲堂，本王睡着的时候都闻过，薄得像一碗刷锅水。这里的，像一口封了几百年的井，刚揭开盖子。」

小满想起了褚先生望着泗水的那双眼睛。他没有再问，把袖子挽起来，顺着崖壁往下爬。他是猎户家的孩子，爬崖是本行，可爬到一半，便觉出这道崖跟蒙山的不一样：蒙山的崖是活的，石缝里长草，草根底下有土；这道崖却是死的，从上到下一根草也不长，石头凉得透骨，凉得像是从来没有晒过一天日头。

爬到底，是一片平地，平地尽头是一面石墙，光秃秃的，一丈来高，两丈来宽，不见门，不见缝，不见花纹。墙脚下东一块西一块地堆着些石头，大大小小，像是从崖上滚下来的。银月道：「那面墙后头，有风。」小满从头上拔下一根头发，捏在指头上，举到墙前。那根头发起先软塌塌地垂着，垂了好一会儿，然后很轻很轻地，往墙的方向飘了一飘，又一飘，倒像墙那边有一张嘴，隔着一层石头，在慢慢地吸气。

小满蹲下身来，把手贴在墙上，一寸一寸地摸过去。他爹教过他摸兽迹：同是一块泥，踩过的和没踩过的，手摸上去不一样。他摸到第三遍，在墙的右下角摸着了一块石头，比旁边的更凉，凉得发麻，四边一道极细的缝，细得指甲都塞不进去。他正要按，那块石头底下，却有一样东西动了一动。

墙角贴着地，有一汪浅浅的小潭，是崖顶上的水一滴一滴积下来的，只有脸盆大小。潭边卧着一块圆石头，白里透青，他方才摸墙的时候，胳膊肘还在上头靠过一靠。这时那块「石头」前头，慢慢地探出一个脑袋来，赤红赤红的，像一颗烧透了的炭，两只小眼睛一眨不眨地盯着他的手。小满的手缩得比兔子还快。猎户家的孩子，头一回把一只活兽当成了一块石头，还拿胳膊肘靠了人家一下，他心里好生惭愧，嘴上道：「……对不住，没瞧见。」那东西不领这个情，脑袋一伸，「喀」的一口，咬住了他的袖口。

银月在他肩上看了半天，道：「白身，赤首，像龟。……叫什么来着。本王年轻的时候，在一座山上见过它们一窝。那座山上多金子，多柳树，山里的人捡它们的壳挂在房梁底下，说是能挡火。……[蛫]{注=gui}。对，叫蛫。」小满拽着袖子往回夺，道：「能挡火，挡不挡人？」银月道：「本王只记得它能挡火。」那蛫咬着袖子不松口，身子往后一坐，竟把他拖了个趔趄，一只脚踩进潭里，凉得他牙根一酸。小满这才明白过来，它为什么偏偏卧在这里：那块凉得发麻的石头，就在它背后。它守的不是一潭水，是这面墙。

他试了三回：伸左手，它咬左手；伸右手，它咬右手；两只手一齐伸，它把脑袋一缩，缩进壳里，那壳硬得像一口倒扣的铁锅。小满甩着手，心里骂了一句「你爷爷的」，却没有动真气。他如今是练气二层，一掌拍下去，这口铁锅未必扛得住；可一掌拍下去，崖顶上若有人探头，看见的便不是一个运气好的外门弟子了。何况他爹说过，不吃的东西，不打。
story.en:
No spirit beast may go into the hidden realm — one whiff of the old pill-dregs in there and it goes mad. Xiaoman had to leave the little zheng at the stewards' office. It clung to his sleeve, all five tails up; Zhou Heng took a radish from his drawer and set it on the corner of the table: "It eats one, I write down one." The zheng stared at the radish with a look that plainly said you'd sell me for one radish — then let go of the sleeve, hopped onto the table and ate it.

On the three hundred steps before the gate Elder Qu was sweeping the three hundredth as always. Three hundred-odd people poured down past him; he didn't look up, only moved his broom aside. On that step Xiaoman slowed. The old man spoke, not loudly, as if to the step: "The water's gone lower than last time." Xiaoman started. Still sweeping, Qu said: "Last time was lower than the time before." "…Is that good or bad?" No answer; the broom moved aside to make a way. "Steady legs." A dozen steps down Xiaoman looked back: the sweeper stood leaning on his broom, looking not at him but at the Si shrunk to a thread below the mountain.

At the hour of the dragon the three hundred-odd outer disciples crowded onto the flats. The mud was black and crusted with white frost, and on the frost lay a few fish that hadn't followed the water, mouths opening and closing as if asking what had happened. The stone door stood out of the mud, wisps of white breath rising from its seam — warm, on a winter morning. Xiaoman smelled it from far off; he couldn't say what it was, only that one breath of it made his heart go still.

Before the door stood a man in a grey robe, mild of face, hands folded in his sleeves: Abbot Xuanchenzi. The seniors said that whenever the realm opened he stood like this from the opening until everyone was in, and on the closing day again from the first one out to the last. Asked what he was doing, he said: counting people. But he never held a book, and never counted aloud.

Sun Ergou squeezed up beside Xiaoman, hands in his sleeves, snot frozen into two shiny icicles. "Brother Shen, can I come with you? My roots are bad, going in alone I'm afraid…" He blushed before he said it: "…afraid of getting stuck to a wall." Xiaoman looked at him. At Sun Ergou's waist hung a blue cloth pouch with a bit of red string — the charm his mother sewed, the one Xiaoman had seen in the cowshed. Xiaoman thought: come with me, and go where? I don't know myself yet. He took a radish from his bundle and put it in Sun Ergou's hand: "More people on the right. More people, nobody dies." "…And you, brother?" "Fewer people for me. Fewer people, nobody dies either." Sun Ergou didn't follow, but he nodded gravely and tucked the radish into his coat beside the charm.

The steward struck the gong three times. The door ground open a crack and three hundred people shoved in, mud flying high. Xiaoman didn't shove. Nor did one other man: of the two map sellers, the one who'd kicked his left ribs stood at the edge of the crowd with his arms folded, watching not the door but him. Xiaoman stood on a rock and waited — his father had taught him: when a herd of deer bolts, never push into it; stand still and let it run past, and the path is clear. When the last one was through, he hopped down and strolled in. Inside, he glanced back: the man with folded arms was strolling in after him.

The moment he stepped through the door, the token on his chest flared hot. Not like before: before, one pulse meant she was awake and had something to say; this time it pulsed and didn't stop — a second, a third, faster and faster, like a heart beating under his own. He drew it out; the silver tail blazed. A half-transparent silver fox slipped out and sat on his shoulder, more solid than before. She didn't yawn; her golden eyes were wide, looking at the walls, the carvings, the flagstones underfoot, nose twitching as if at something far, far away.

When she spoke, her voice had changed, like someone standing in the yard she lived in as a child: "…This place. I have been here." "When?" "I don't know." "What for?" "I don't know." "Then what do you know?" Her nose twitched twice more before she said: "…Left."

The road on the map went right. Three hundred people went right along the corridor, clattering, their voices crashing off the walls. To the left was a narrow crack in the rock, half blocked by a fallen boulder with a crooked word cut in it — DANGER — and under it a skull, and in the skull's eye sockets someone had added two charcoal tears. On the map, beside the crack, another note: "Left cliff. Sticky. Three stuck ten years ago, three days; one came out mad." Xiaoman folded the map, tucked it away and squeezed in sideways.

Behind the crack a flight of steps went down, narrow, steep, wet, thick with moss. After about the time of a meal it ended at a drop; below was black, only the sound of water dripping, one drop, a long pause, another. "Down," said Yinyue. "There's nothing down there." "I don't know what's down there. I know the spirit-qi here comes up from below." She paused, and her voice dropped: "…Thick qi. The river outside, the mountain, the lecture hall — I've smelled them in my sleep, thin as dishwater. This is like a well sealed for hundreds of years, its lid just lifted."

Xiaoman remembered Master Chu's eyes looking toward the Si. He asked no more, rolled up his sleeves and climbed down. A hunter's son, climbing was his trade; but halfway down he felt this cliff was not like Meng Mountain's. Those cliffs were alive, grass in the cracks, soil under the roots; this one was dead, not one blade of grass top to bottom, the stone cold to the bone, as if no sun had ever touched it.

At the bottom was a flat floor, and at its end a stone wall, bare, ten feet high, twenty wide, no door, no crack, no carving. Stones lay scattered at its foot, big and small, as if rolled down from the cliff. "Behind that wall," said Yinyue, "there's wind." Xiaoman pulled out a hair and held it up before the wall. It hung limp a good while; then very, very lightly it drifted toward the wall, and again, as if a mouth on the other side were slowly breathing in through the stone.

Xiaoman crouched and ran his palm along the wall inch by inch. His father had taught him to feel tracks: the same mud trodden and untrodden feels different to the hand. On the third pass, at the bottom right, he found a stone colder than the rest, cold enough to numb, with a hairline seam round it too fine for a fingernail. He was about to press it when something under it moved.

Against the wall, at floor level, lay a shallow little pool, gathered drop by drop from the cliff above, no bigger than a washbasin. Beside it sat a round stone, white shading to green; he had leaned his elbow on it a moment ago. Now from the front of that "stone" a head slowly pushed out, red as a coal burned through, two small eyes fixed unblinking on his hand. Xiaoman snatched his hand back faster than a rabbit. A hunter's son, and for the first time in his life he'd taken a live beast for a rock — and leaned his elbow on it. He was ashamed, and said: "…Sorry, didn't see you." The thing wasn't having it: its head shot out and — snap — it had his cuff.

Yinyue looked a long while from his shoulder. "White body, red head, like a turtle… what was it called. When I was young I saw a nest of them on a mountain. Lots of gold there, lots of willows; the mountain folk picked up their shells and hung them under the roof beams, said they kept off fire. …A gui. Yes, a gui." Tugging at his sleeve, Xiaoman said: "It keeps off fire — does it keep off people?" "I only remember it keeps off fire." The gui held on and sat back, dragging him off balance so one foot went into the pool, so cold his teeth ached. Then Xiaoman understood why it lay just here: the numbing-cold stone was right behind it. It wasn't guarding a pool. It was guarding the wall.

He tried three times: left hand, it bit the left; right hand, it bit the right; both hands, it pulled its head in, and the shell was hard as an iron pot turned upside down. Xiaoman shook out his hands and swore to himself — your grandpa's — but didn't use his true qi. At layer two now, one blow might crack that pot; but one blow, and if anyone looked over the cliff top, what they'd see would no longer be a lucky outer disciple. Besides, his father said: what you won't eat, you don't hit.

exits.means: has solved the nine squares and goes through the wall

refuse.zh: 九个格子还没填对。墙不动。
refuse.en: The nine squares are not right yet. The wall does not move.

story.zh:
他想起他爹的另一句话：「乌龟缩头，你跟它比耐性，比不过的。你把它翻过来。」他便蹲在潭边，一动不动，像在蒙山上蹲鹿。蹲了约莫一炷香，那颗赤红的脑袋又一点一点探了出来，左看看，右看看。便在它看右边的那一霎，小满左手往它鼻子前一晃，它一口咬了个空；他右手已扣住了壳沿，「嘿」的一声，把它整个儿掀了个底朝天。

那蛫仰面躺在石地上，四只脚在半空里乱划。小满站起身，正要去按那块石头，眼角却扫到了那汪小潭。潭边的石头上，一圈一圈，全是水印子：最高的一圈，齐他的膝盖；往下一圈，齐他的小腿；再往下，齐他的脚踝。最底下那汪水，如今只剩一巴掌深。他想起瞿老扫着台阶说的话：水，退得比上回低；上回比上上回低。这东西守着这面墙，守着这一巴掌水，也不知守了多少年。

他又想起药园里那只小狰：偷来的，怎么吃都吃不饱；给的，一根就饱了。他弯下腰，把那蛫翻了回来，捧着放回潭里，又解下腰上的竹筒，拔了塞子，把里头的水一口不剩，全倒了进去。潭水涨了一指。银月道：「那是你三天的水。」小满道：「墙后头有风，风里有潮气。有潮气，就有水。」他把空竹筒挂回腰上，又道，「没有，就算我欠它的。」

那蛫泡在水里，一双小眼睛瞅着他，眨了两眨，然后慢慢挪开身子，把那块凉得发麻的石头让了出来。石头巴掌大，石面上有九道浅浅的凹痕，横三竖三，磨得几乎平了——墙上不见花纹，花纹在这里。九道凹痕里各卧着一枚石子，刻着点数，却摆得乱七八糟。小满看着那九个格子，想起了灶间的油灯，想起了九颗刻了记号的栗子，想起了他娘一面纳鞋底一面哼的那句：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」他把刻着五点的那枚石子，挪到了正中。银月在他肩上嘀咕了一句：「有本书叫《山海经》{典=shanhai-gui}，写它『其狀如龜，而白身赤首』，『是可以禦火』——写书那人蹲在即公山上看了它们三天，本王看了他三天。书上没写它会守墙。」

他按了下去。只听得「轰隆隆——」一阵闷响，从墙根底下一直响到崖顶上，那面墙从正中裂开了一道缝，一股风从缝里涌出来，扑在他脸上，暖得像春天。

便在这时，头顶上传来一阵脚步声，碎石子一阵一阵往下落。「——我就说他往这边走了！」
story.en:
He remembered another saying of his father's: "When a turtle pulls its head in, you won't out-wait it. Turn it over." So he crouched by the pool, motionless, as if waiting for deer on Meng Mountain. After about a stick of incense the red head crept out bit by bit, looking left, looking right. The instant it looked right, Xiaoman's left hand flicked before its nose — it bit air — and his right hand had the rim of the shell. "Hup!" and over it went, belly up.

The gui lay on its back, four legs paddling the air. Xiaoman stood, about to press the stone, when his eye fell on the pool. The rock round it was ringed with water marks: the highest at his knee, the next at his shin, the next at his ankle. What was left at the bottom was a hand's depth. He remembered Elder Qu at his sweeping: the water's gone lower than last time; last time lower than the time before. This creature had been guarding this wall and this handful of water for who knew how many years.

And he remembered the little zheng in the herb garden: what it stole never filled it; what it was given, one filled it. He bent, turned the gui back over, set it in the pool, unslung the bamboo flask at his waist, pulled the stopper and poured in every drop. The pool rose a finger's width. "That was your three days' water," said Yinyue. "There's wind behind the wall, and damp in the wind. Where there's damp there's water." He hung the empty flask back on his belt. "If there isn't, I owe it."

The gui lay in the water and looked at him with its small eyes, blinked twice, then slowly moved aside and left the numbing-cold stone clear. It was the size of a palm, with nine shallow hollows worn almost flat, three by three — no carving on the wall; the carving was here. In each hollow sat a pebble marked with dots, all in the wrong places. Xiaoman looked at the nine squares and thought of the oil lamp in the kitchen, the nine marked chestnuts, and the rhyme his mother hummed over her sole-stitching: "Nine on the head, one on the feet, three on the left, seven on the right, two and four the shoulders, six and eight the feet, five in the middle." He moved the pebble with five dots to the centre. Yinyue muttered on his shoulder: "There's a book called the Classic of Mountains and Seas that says it is 'shaped like a turtle, white body and red head' and 'wards off fire' — the man who wrote it squatted on Mount Jigong watching them for three days, and I watched him for three days. The book doesn't say it guards walls."

He pressed. A deep rumble ran from the foot of the wall right up the cliff; the wall split down the middle and a wind poured through the crack into his face, warm as spring.

Just then footsteps sounded overhead and pebbles came rattling down. "— I told you he went this way!"

withdrawn.en: The gui draws back into the pool, then pokes its red head out again and stares at you unblinking. — Again.
